Her group's work on cross-lingual audio-visual speech representation learning [paper:W4402684056] connects to my wav2vec2-style Tamil speech model [lib:cv], while the study of LLM-guided MT post-editing with error annotations [paper:W4401042399] informs how I think about targeted adaptation versus expensive fine-tuning — the same tradeoff I encountered adapting Kannada tokenizers at Microsoft Research India [lib:cv]. Her CHI 2025 paper examining generative AI design for non-native speakers [paper:W4409736318] aligns with my goal of evaluation that goes beyond translated benchmarks and measures real user needs [lib:interests].

Prof. Rudinger's work on evaluation methodology for LLMs [advisor:Rachel Rudinger] connects directly to my interest in moving beyond translated English benchmarks [lib:interests]. Her ACL 2025 paper diagnosing flaws in multiple-choice LLM evaluation and proposing fixes [paper:W4412886673] resonates with the gaps I observed building the Tamil–English code-switched test set, where standard metrics masked an 18–26 point performance drop [lib:cv]. Her collaboration with Prof. Carpuat on paraphrastic variability in reasoning errors [paper:W4402640336] also suggests a productive path toward understanding why multilingual models fail on code-switched inputs — a question I want to pursue in my PhD [lib:interests].

Prof. Wiegreffe's research on mechanistic interpretability and the faithfulness of natural language explanations [advisor:Sarah Wiegreffe] speaks to my secondary interest in evaluation that measures faithfulness rather than surface accuracy [lib:interests]. Her work interrogating what 'mechanistic' actually means for explanation methods [paper:W4404784049] and her findings on easy training data for hard tasks [paper:W4401042639] raise questions I find relevant when asking why tokenizer-adapted Kannada models improve on QA but may still fail on culturally grounded prompts [lib:cv]. Understanding internal model behavior could complement the black-box evaluation work I have done so far [lib:cv].

sop.text:
I am applying to the PhD program in Computer Science to work on multilingual natural language processing — specifically, making large language models genuinely useful for the hundreds of millions of people who speak Indian languages but are poorly served by today's models.

My interest began with a concrete failure. In 2025, while working in Prof. S. Venkatesan's multilingual NLP lab at NIT Trichy, I built a Tamil–English code-switched evaluation set of 2,400 sentences [lib:cv]. Two open 7B models lost 18–26 points relative to monolingual Tamil baselines on those inputs [lib:cv]. People in Chennai do not speak monolingual Tamil to a chatbot; they switch. That result became my first-author workshop paper at an ACL-family Student Research Workshop in 2026 [lib:cv], and it convinced me that evaluation design — not just model training — is where multilingual NLP is most broken [lib:interests].

At Microsoft Research India in summer 2026, mentored by Dr. Anjali Mehra, I worked on the adaptation side of the same problem [lib:cv]. Extending a SentencePiece vocabulary with 6,000 Kannada-specific tokens cut average token count per sentence by 41% and improved downstream QA F1 by 3.4 points at an identical fine-tuning budget [lib:cv]. That result sharpened a working hypothesis I want to pursue in a PhD: targeted, parameter-efficient interventions — in the tokenizer, in the prompt, in selected layers — can close gaps that brute-force scaling does not [lib:interests].

A third thread came from a Spring 2026 course project in which I trained a small wav2vec2-style model on 40 hours of Tamil radio audio and reached 31% WER on a held-out set [lib:cv]. Tamil, like many Indian languages, has far more spoken data than clean written text; speech-to-text pipelines are therefore an essential part of any realistic deployment [lib:interests]. I want to understand how speech representations interact with the cross-lingual alignment properties of multilingual LLMs.

In a PhD I want to pursue three connected questions: (1) How can parameter-efficient fine-tuning and tokenizer adaptation be combined with principled data selection to adapt LLMs to low-resource Indian languages without catastrophic forgetting? (2) What evaluation protocols actually capture code-switching ability, cultural grounding, and faithfulness for multilingual users, rather than relying on translated English benchmarks? (3) How can speech-text models be made robust to the noise and code-switching characteristic of real spoken Indian-language data?

UMD's CS department is where I want to pursue these questions. Prof. Marine Carpuat's CLIP Lab works directly on cross-lingual generalization, speech-translation quality estimation, and human-centered evaluation of AI for non-native speakers [advisor:Marine Carpuat] — all three of my core directions. Her group's work on LLM-guided MT post-editing with error annotations [paper:W4401042399] and on AI design for non-native speakers [paper:W4409736318] reflects exactly the combination of system-building and evaluation rigor I am aiming for. I am also drawn to Prof. Rachel Rudinger's work on evaluation methodology [advisor:Rachel Rudinger]; her diagnosis of flaws in multiple-choice LLM evaluation [paper:W4412886673] and her collaboration on paraphrastic variability in reasoning errors [paper:W4402640336] raise questions directly relevant to understanding where multilingual evaluation protocols fail.

I bring a 9.21/10 CGPA (top 5% of my department) [lib:profile], a peer-reviewed first-author publication [lib:cv], two research experiences that together cover evaluation and adaptation [lib:cv], and practical experience as a TA for a 120-student machine learning course [lib:cv]. I also organize NIT Trichy's NLP reading group of roughly 25 members [lib:cv]. I am prepared to contribute to and benefit from the research environment at UMD from Fall 2027.

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student (Fall 2027) — multilingual LLM adaptation and evaluation
emails.body:
Dear Prof. Carpuat,

I am a final-year B.Tech student in Computer Science at NIT Tiruchirappalli (expected graduation May 2027) applying to the UMD CS PhD program for Fall 2027 entry. I am writing to ask whether you are planning to take new PhD students in this cycle.

My work sits at the intersection of your CLIP Lab's interests. I built a Tamil–English code-switched evaluation set showing 18–26 point drops in open 7B models and published the findings as a first-author workshop paper. At Microsoft Research India this past summer I worked on Kannada tokenizer adaptation, cutting token counts by 41% and improving QA F1 by 3.4 points at the same fine-tuning budget.

I read your CHI 2025 paper "Sustaining Human Agency, Attending to Its Cost" with Prof. Xiao and colleagues carefully; the framework for evaluating AI support for non-native speakers maps directly onto what I think is missing from current multilingual LLM evaluation.

I would be glad to share my CV if that would be helpful. Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
Priya Raman

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student (Fall 2027) — LLM evaluation methodology
emails.body:
Dear Prof. Rudinger,

I am a final-year B.Tech student in Computer Science at NIT Tiruchirappalli applying to the UMD CS PhD program for Fall 2027. Your profile page indicates you are planning to admit students for this cycle, which encouraged me to write.

My research focuses on evaluation gaps in multilingual LLMs: I built a Tamil–English code-switched test set that exposed 18–26 point performance drops invisible to standard benchmarks, leading to a first-author workshop paper in 2026. I want to develop evaluation protocols that measure cultural grounding and code-switching robustness rather than relying on translated English benchmarks.

Your ACL 2025 paper "Which of These Best Describes Multiple Choice Evaluation with LLMs?" — diagnosing and proposing fixes for structural flaws in standard evaluation — is directly relevant to the problems I keep running into when evaluating models on Tamil and Kannada inputs. I would value the chance to discuss this further.

I have attached my CV for your reference. Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
Priya Raman

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student (Fall 2027) — interpretability and evaluation
emails.body:
Dear Prof. Wiegreffe,

I am a final-year B.Tech student in Computer Science at NIT Tiruchirappalli applying to the UMD CS PhD program for Fall 2027. I am writing to ask whether you are planning to take new PhD students in this cycle.

My primary focus is multilingual LLM adaptation and evaluation for Indian languages, but I have a strong secondary interest in understanding why models fail — mechanistically, not just behaviorally. At Microsoft Research India I observed that tokenizer adaptation improved QA F1 without any obvious change to the fine-tuning procedure, and I have no principled explanation for where in the model that improvement originates.

Your 2024 paper "Mechanistic?" with Prof. Saphra, which interrogates what mechanistic interpretability methods actually establish, raises exactly the methodological questions I think matter for understanding multilingual model behavior rather than just measuring it.

I would be happy to share my CV if useful. Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
Priya Raman
